history.heading: Peoples of the forest
paragraphs: Gabon, on the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, has been inhabited for tens of thousands of years, first by forest peoples (often called Pygmies) and later by Bantu-speaking groups such as the Fang, Myene, Punu and Nzebi. The Lopé-Okanda landscape contains ancient rock art and archaeological sites.
Portuguese navigators arrived in 1472, naming the estuary after the shape of a hooded cloak, gabão. The coast became involved in the slave trade and later in trade in ivory and timber.

history.heading: French colony
paragraphs: France established a presence in the 1840s, and Libreville was founded in 1849 by freed slaves. Gabon became part of French Equatorial Africa. Albert Schweitzer founded his famous hospital in Lambaréné in 1913.

history.heading: The Bongo era and the 2023 coup
paragraphs: Gabon became independent on 17 August 1960. Omar Bongo became president in 1967 and ruled for 41 years, keeping close ties with France and using oil wealth to maintain power. His son Ali Bongo succeeded him in 2009.

In August 2023, after Ali Bongo was declared winner of a disputed election, the military seized power, ending the family's 56-year rule. General Brice Oligui Nguema led a transition and was elected president in April 2025.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: French is the official language, and Fang is the most widely spoken local language. Most people are Christian. Bwiti, a spiritual practice using the iboga plant, is an important tradition.
Gabonese masks, such as those of the Punu and Kota peoples, influenced European artists like Picasso. Food includes nyembwe (chicken in palm nut sauce), cassava and plantains.

politics.heading: Transition
paragraphs: Following the 2023 coup, a new constitution adopted by referendum in 2024 established a presidential system without a prime minister, with seven-year terms. Oligui Nguema won the 2025 presidential election by a large margin. Observers watch whether the transition leads to real democratic reform.

economy.heading: Oil and forests
paragraphs: Gabon is one of the wealthier countries in sub-Saharan Africa per person, thanks to oil, manganese (it is a top world producer) and timber. However, wealth is unevenly distributed, and a large share of the population is poor.

Gabon is about 88 percent covered by rainforest and has a network of national parks protecting forest elephants and gorillas. It has received payments for reducing carbon emissions and carried out a debt-for-nature swap. The currency is the Central African CFA franc.
